newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish business urges elections this year.
newsitem.headline: Turkish business urges elections this year.

text.p: The Turkish government's plan for early elections has clouded the prospects for an improvement in the economy and businessmen are urging the cabinet to hold polls as soon as possible.
"To delay the election date will be harmful for our economy. It must be held this year," Selim Yasar, chairman of the Aegean Chamber of Industry, said in a statement.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist-led coalition government has unveiled plans for early elections, though no specific date has been determined by the coalition partners as yet. A general electionwould normally be due by 2000.
In the meantime the government is unlikely to take unpopular but long-awaited structural measures, strongly needed to reduce large public spending and trade deficits.
On the contrary, it is expected to boost public spending and farm subsidies and delay state-sector price hikes to help win the elections.

"Elections mean monetary expansion and destruction of economic parameters. However it is also important to know when the elections will be held. Because uncertainties also damage the economy as much as elections do," Tayyar Ozturk, general manager of Ekinciler Securities, said.

Increased pre-election public spending, accompanied by the military's strong cash need to fund its operations againts rebel Kurds in northern Iraq, may accelerate the fiscal deterioration and widen public deficits, now around 10 percent of gross domestic product.
Finance Minister Abdullatif Sener said the government might seek to prepare a supplementary budget later this year to finance "unforeseen spending".
However, businessmen and bankers believe an early poll held this year would have less impact on the economy than one held in 1998.

By the end of October the treasury's domestic debt service burden will fall. The central bank's high foreign currency reserves of around $16.5 billion, a seasonally lower pace of inflation and higher foreign exchange inflow in summer months indicate that the economy will suffer less from a 1997 election.

"If Turkey takes a decision for early elections, it must do it as soon as possible. A March election is the worse of all alternatives. Because the fiscal imbalances will have been extended for one more year," said Sinan Gumusdis, treasurer of Chase Manhattan's Istanbul branch.
Turkish newspapers report that the coalition's junior partner True Path Party (DYP) favours March 1998 as the election date while Erbakan's Welfare Party urges elections this year.
But even some members of the DYP express the same concern -- the later the elections, the bigger the damage to the economy.

"Elections will not bring any benefit to the economy. But they will eliminate the uncertainty and turmoil in politics. Having them in the shortest possible term will do the minimum damage to the economy," Ufuk Soylemez, state minister from the coalition's DYP wing, said at the weekend.
Gumusdis said the treasury's relatively higher domestic debt servicing in the first quarter of 1998 raised the fears that any election in March would create more damage for the economy.

Almost all the economists and bankers agree that inflation, now running at around 80 percent, will jump in the aftermath of elections -- whenever they are held -- because of high pre-election spending and lax monetary and fiscal policies.
